ai_summary: Great Britain's wind fleet is currently generating 5.0 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output contributing 1.8 GW, representing 17.8% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Despite this modest operational level, Scotland maintains an optimal carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh, contrasting sharply with the GB-wide figure of 194 gCO2/kWh. Structural transmission bottlenecks continue to limit the transfer of clean northern generation to southern demand centers. Consequently, 578 MWh of Scottish generation has been curtailed so far today, incurring a direct constraint cost of about £38,647. To replace this trapped zero-carbon power, fossil generation was dispatched elsewhere on the system, resulting in an estimated 109,801 m3 of gas burned and adding 202 tonnes of CO2 to the atmosphere. Extrapolating today's figures indicates an estimated total yearly cost of curtailment of roughly £14 million. Across nationwide consumer demand, this level of grid friction is estimated to increase everybody's invoice in the UK by approximately £0.05/MWh, illustrating how localized grid constraints impose both an environmental penalty and an avoidable financial surcharge on all British billpayers.
